extract:
The Rolling Stones formed in London in 1962, emerging from the city's burgeoning rhythm and blues club scene centered on venues like the Ealing Jazz Club and the Crawdaddy Club in Richmond. Active for more than six decades, they rank among the longest-running and most successful bands in rock history, outlasting nearly all of their British Invasion contemporaries.

The band's core came together when childhood acquaintances Mick Jagger and Keith Richards reconnected on a Dartford railway platform in 1961, bonding over records by Chuck Berry and Muddy Waters, whose song "Rollin' Stone" gave the group its name. Guitarist Brian Jones, a devoted blues purist, founded the group and recruited pianist Ian Stewart. Bassist Bill Wyman and drummer Charlie Watts completed the classic lineup by early 1963. Encouraged by Alexis Korner's Blues Incorporated, a key incubator for London's blues scene, the band built a following before manager Andrew Loog Oldham signed them to Decca Records in the UK, with London Records handling American releases. Oldham also produced their early recordings and cultivated their image as a scruffy, menacing counterpoint to the Beatles.

Their early output leaned heavily on covers. The 1964 debut The Rolling Stones (issued in the US as England's Newest Hitmakers) featured songs by Bo Diddley, Willie Dixon, and Slim Harpo, while the Five by Five EP and 12 X 5 captured sessions at Chicago's Chess Studios, the home of their idols. Oldham pushed Jagger and Richards to write their own material, and the payoff arrived with "The Last Time" and especially "(I Can't Get No) Satisfaction," whose fuzz-toned Richards riff powered Out Of Our Heads in 1965 to international success. Aftermath (1966) was their first album consisting entirely of Jagger-Richards originals, with Jones adding sitar to "Paint It, Black" and marimba and dulcimer elsewhere, signaling a broadening palette. Later landmarks included Beggars Banquet (1968), Let It Bleed (1969), Sticky Fingers (1971), and Exile on Main St. (1972), several produced by Jimmy Miller, with tracks like "Sympathy for the Devil," "Gimme Shelter," and "Brown Sugar."

The lineup shifted over the years. Jones was dismissed in 1969 and died weeks later, replaced by Mick Taylor, who in turn gave way to Ronnie Wood in 1975. In 1970 the band launched their own Rolling Stones Records with its famous tongue-and-lips logo. Their era was shadowed by drug arrests and the 1969 Altamont concert, where a fan was killed during their set, an event documented in the film Gimme Shelter.

Critics have long regarded the band's late-sixties and early-seventies run as one of rock's greatest stretches, and they were inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame in 1989. Their stadium tours set attendance and revenue records repeatedly, establishing the template for the modern rock spectacle.

Charlie Watts died in 2021, with Steve Jordan taking over on drums for touring. In 2023 the band released Hackney Diamonds, their first album of original material since 2005's A Bigger Bang, produced by Andrew Watt and featuring Paul McCartney, Elton John, Lady Gaga, and Stevie Wonder. It earned a Grammy for Best Rock Album, and Jagger, Richards, and Wood continue to tour.
title: The Rolling Stones
